The screening would check pilots for any prohibited substances and medications under ​ aviation regulations, as per the internal communication. The tests will be conducted alongside training sessions at ​Air India's academy in Gurugram, or post-flight at the airline's briefing centres and offices, reports said. Under the existing rules, airlines carry out random testing of at least least 10% of their flight crew for ​psychoactive substances each year.. "We nevertheless now feel that it is important to go further," Reuters cited the internal email from Air India as saying. The decision comes as Indian aviation authorities probe an incident involving an Air India flight from Phuket to New Delhi on August 4, which suddenly lost about 300 feet (91 meters) of altitude, injuring 20 passengers and four crew members. The captain of the Airbus A320neo tested positive for marijuana in a confirmatory drug test following the incident. Thursday's agitation came in opposition to the Cauvery Water Regulation Committee directing Karnataka to release 12,000 cusecs of Cauvery river's water to the neighboring state of Tamil Nadu for 15 days. Protesters have called on the Karnataka government to not release the water saying the state itself is facing water shortages, particularly for drinking and irrigation requirements. The dispute over sharing the water of the 765-kilometer (475-mile) long river, which resurfaces during rainfall deficit years, dates back a century and has also witnessed bloodshed in the past. On Thursday, security measures were tightened in several places in the state, including in Mandya, one of the districts associated with the longstanding issue. According to news agency PTI, the shutdown was met with a mixed response with protests in Mandya and preventive detentions at various locations. However, urban areas like Bengaluru and Mysuru remained unaffected after organizations that had earlier backed the shutdown, pulled away their support. https://p.dw.com/p/5Ik0A Skip next section Protests mark monsoon session of parliament 08/13/2026 August 13, 2026 Protests mark monsoon session of parliament On the very first day of the monsoon session on July 20, parliament was rocked by a massive youth-led march trying to get to its gates as part of the Cockroach Janta Party movement demanding the resignation of the now former education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over exam irregularities. The protesters were met with baton-charges and tear gas firing , and since then the opposition has railed against the violent crackdown, demanding an answer in the parliament from Union Home Minister Amit Shah over alleged police brutality. On Wednesday, Shah said that the Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government was ready for a discussion on the student protests which were triggered by a slew of medical entrance exam paper leaks. The leader of the opposition in the Lok Sabha, Congress's Rahul Gandhi, turned down the debate offer saying that the youth wanted answers on who ordered the use of force on protesters and "not a lecture" from Shah. Addressing a press conference on Thursday, Union Minister of Parliamentarty Affairs Kiren Rijiju accused the opposition of "running away from discussions" and alleged that opposition disruptions affected parliament's productivity. During the 19-day monsoon session several demonstrations were held by the Congress-led alliance of opposition parties called the INDIA bloc on the parliament premises against the police action and a d onation embezzlement controversy linked to the Ram Temple , a shrine central to Modi's Hindu-first politics. Lawmakers from Modi's ruling coalition also began staging their own demonstrations, including on the last day over another student protest in Jharkhand — where the Congress party is an ally of the ruling coalition. Tear gas, batons and water cannons were also used to disperse the protesters marching towards the state assembly in Ranchi. https://p.dw.com/p/5Ijws Skip next section Political deadlock rife as parliament's monsoon session ends 08/13/2026 August 13, 2026 Political deadlock rife as parliament's monsoon session ends India's parliament convened on Thursday for the final day of its monsoon session amid an unrelenting political standoff between the government and the opposition. Image: Reuters/Anatolii Stepanov world Russia pounds Kyiv, kills 10 as Ukraine appeals for Patriot interceptors Aug. 2 05:10 am JST Aug. 2 | 12:42 pm JST 13 Comments By Olena Harmash and Yurii Kovalenko KYIV Russia pounded Kyiv and the region in a heavy ballistic missile attack early on Saturday, killing 10 people, as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Ukraine ‌had run out of interceptor missiles for its U.S. Patriot air defense systems. Zelenskyy said that Russia launched 35 missiles at Ukraine, including 27 ballistic missiles, and also 185 drones. Only one ballistic missile was intercepted, "simply because there are no interceptors for the Patriot system", ‌he said. More than a dozen explosions reverberated through the city during several waves ⁠of attacks, according to Reuters witnesses. "Every package of ballistic missile interceptors saves the lives ⁠of our people. And ⁠every night without them results in more casualties," Zelenskyy said on the Telegram app. With the war in its ‌fifth year, fighting is raging along about 1,200 kilometers of front line. But Russian advances have slowed by ⁠more than half this year, and Ukraine has been ⁠launching strikes inside Russia hitting its oil facilities, logistics sites and weapons production. Ukraine was bringing back war to Russia, Zelenskyy said, adding that his troops struck the infrastructure of three oil refineries in the Bashkortostan region and other targets that sustained Moscow's war effort. Russia has also intensified its attacks on ⁠Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities. Ukraine relies on U.S.-made Patriot air defense systems, but the Iran war ⁠has seen supplies of interceptor missiles previously earmarked ‌for Ukraine diverted to the U.S. military and U.S. allies in the Gulf. Moscow and Kyiv both deny targeting civilians in the war launched by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. SECOND MAJOR ATTACK ON KYIV THIS WEEK Saturday's is the second major attack on Kyiv this week after nine people, including six members of one family ‌in a village near Kryvyi Rih, were killed on Thursday and a suspected Russian cruise missile landed in Poland. Damage was recorded in seven districts across Kyiv, a city of about 3 million people, the Prosecutor's General Office said after Saturday's attacks. Zelenskiy said that fires broke out across Kyiv and 18 residential buildings, a school, the Lithuanian Embassy, and infrastructure facilities were damaged. Ukrainian prosecutors said seven people were killed in the Darnytskyi district on the left bank of the Dnipro river and two more people died in the Solomyanskyi district on the right bank ​of the city. One more person was killed in the Kyiv region where the attacks damaged several warehouses, regional officials said. Dozens of people in Kyiv and the region were injured, including four children who suffered ‌multiple shrapnel wounds and lacerations. "I looked at my phone, it was 1:30 (22:30 GMT) and sirens (blared), I was lying dressed in my bed, I got up immediately. And at once explosions started - boom, boom," said Nadiia Komarova, a 68-year-old concierge at an apartment building in ‌Kyiv. "Our ceilings have started to crumble. My window here is smashed, and everything has fallen inside," she ⁠told Reuters. Reuters television footage showed police and ⁠rescuers working on the site. Two rescuers put a ​body in a black sack in a car. Firefighters were extinguishing fires and charred cars stood ⁠near an apartment building. Mayor Vitali Klitschko said ‌Kyiv was working to build and prepare more shelters as attacks continue to ​intensify. Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha issued a fresh plea for urgent air defense supplies. "It is the battle for the skies that will define the trajectory of this war. The stronger the air shield over Ukraine, the closer peace becomes." © Thomson Reuters 2026. ©2026 GPlusMedia Inc.
